title: MEGA lab: NJ vs UPGMA on vertebrate globins
summary: Reproduce three MEGA 12 runs on a 23-sequence vertebrate globin alignment — Poisson distances under pairwise deletion, then a Neighbor-Joining tree and a UPGMA tree on the same matrix — matching MEGA-CC 12.1.4's numbers end to end.

source.citation: The UniProt Consortium, UniProt: the Universal Protein Knowledgebase in 2025, Nucleic Acids Research 53 (D1). https://www.uniprot.org

prompts.concept: The closest pair in this matrix is tempting — two of the 23 sequences are identical over every kept site, as close as a pair can be. Does this method join the closest pair first? Pick a cell in the matrix, or click two leaves.
prompts.math: NJ joins the pair minimizing Q(i,j) = (n-2)·d(i,j) - R_i - R_j. Each cluster's total distance to everything else counts, not just the pair's own distance — a pair far from the rest can outscore a merely-close pair. UPGMA asks the simpler question — it joins the closest pair in the current matrix, every step.
prompts.reveal: Under NJ on the Poisson matrix — the lab's run — Human_HBA and Horse_HBA, two mammalian alpha globins, join first under Q, even though the closest pair in the matrix is Human_HBB and Chimp_HBB, identical over every kept site: the beta pair sits among its beta relatives, and Q weighs each cluster's total distance to everything else. On the JTT matrix the same Q rule opens with Cow_HBA and Human_HBA instead. Under UPGMA — the handout's step-4 switch — the closest pair joins, so the identical betas open that tree.

prompts.concept: This is the NJ run's last join: past it the finished tree is an unrooted NJ tree. On a UPGMA run this position is still mid-run — two of its 22 merges remain. Read the finished NJ tree by its splits: the six alpha globins together (the four mammalian alphas with chicken and Xenopus alpha); the ten mammalian beta globins together — the identical human–chimp betas and the cow–sheep pair inside it, the mouse–rat pair on the next split out to make all twelve mammalian betas; and the human gamma gene, the three non-mammal betas (chicken, Xenopus, zebrafish) and myoglobin stepping off between the two big groups.
prompts.math: Every internal edge of an unrooted tree defines a split; two trees are the same tree exactly when their split sets match. The handout's next step re-runs this matrix under UPGMA — a rooted, clock-assuming method: compare the groupings, not the way either program draws the tree.

lab.title: MEGA: NJ vs UPGMA on vertebrate globins
objectives: Run MEGA's distance → tree chain under the Poisson model on a 23-taxon globin alignment, once with Neighbor-Joining and once with UPGMA
Match each MEGA analysis option to the NeoPhylo control that reproduces it
See where a clock-assuming method and Neighbor-Joining agree — and where an exact tie lets two valid trees differ
lab.handout_md:
## What this lab reproduces

The second classic MEGA chain: one pairwise-distance matrix under the Poisson model on a protein alignment, then two trees on that same matrix — a Neighbor-Joining tree and a UPGMA tree — every option set as the settings table lists it, so the numbers you reproduce are MEGA's own, recorded from MEGA-CC 12.1.4.

## The data

23 vertebrate globin sequences — the alpha and beta globins of mammals, chicken and Xenopus, a zebrafish beta globin, plus human gamma globin and myoglobin — over 156 aligned amino-acid sites. The sequences are UniProtKB records aligned with MAFFT, bundled as the `globins` library dataset.

To cross-check in MEGA itself: load this lab, export the alignment as `.meg` from NeoPhylo's Export menu, open that file in MEGA, and apply the settings table exactly — the distance run first, then each tree run.

## Why Poisson, not JTT

MEGA's "Poisson model" is the correction NeoPhylo calls Poisson, so the numbers here reproduce exactly. MEGA's own JTT estimator is a different calculation from the JTT NeoPhylo ships (the "Coming from MEGA?" guide has the details), so the handout's runs use the model that matches.

## Before you start

Read the settings table. In MEGA each run's options live in the analysis dialog you reach from the menu path in the second column; the table lists every option the runs set — nothing is left to a default — next to the NeoPhylo control that reproduces it.

## Steps

1. Load this lab. NeoPhylo loads the alignment and computes the Poisson matrix — the distance run — under pairwise deletion, MEGA's default gap treatment.
2. Look at the matrix before the tree. Which pair looks closest? Write your prediction down — NJ does not always join the closest pair first.
3. Step through the joins and read the finished NJ tree as unrooted: which globin groups does it contain?
4. Switch the Method control to UPGMA — the second tree run — and build the tree again. UPGMA returns a rooted tree, every leaf the same height from the root: it assumes a molecular clock. Read it as a rooted tree.
5. Compare the two trees' groupings: which do they share, and where do they disagree?

## Questions

- Both methods started from the same matrix; UPGMA joins the closest pair at every step while NJ scores each pair by Q. Did the trees agree on the big groupings — the alpha globins, the mammalian beta globins? Where did they disagree?
- Under pairwise deletion the three mammalian alpha-globin pairs are exactly tied in this matrix. What did each program do with the tie? If another run resolved it differently, would either tree be wrong?
- UPGMA assumes a molecular clock — equal rates on every lineage — and returns a rooted tree; NJ does not. Which differences between the two trees could that assumption explain, and which could it not?
- In the sandbox, switch the gap treatment to Complete deletion: how many columns does this alignment lose, and does either tree change?

lab.mega_note_md:
MEGA's distance output is a lower-triangle text matrix — one row per added taxon, every cell printed to 8 decimals, with `n/c` where a distance cannot be estimated (not an issue here: every pair of the 23 sequences has comparable sites). NeoPhylo draws the full square matrix as a heatmap: cells read to 3 decimals on screen, and a cell that cannot be estimated shows ∞.

MEGA's two tree runs draw differently in its Tree Explorer: the NJ tree opens with an arbitrary root, while the UPGMA tree opens rooted — every leaf the same height above the root, the clock assumption drawn. NeoPhylo draws the NJ tree from an arbitrary root too — the unrooted tree drawn from a point; read it as unrooted — and the UPGMA tree rooted, every leaf the same height. Compare the groupings, not the way either program happens to draw them.

On this data the NJ tree is MEGA's, split for split. The UPGMA tree may differ in one join: under pairwise deletion the three mammalian alpha-globin pairs are exactly tied in the matrix, and any of the tied pairs is a valid UPGMA merge — MEGA's run and NeoPhylo's may resolve the tie differently. Both are valid UPGMA trees for the same matrix; the difference is the tie, not a discrepancy.
